 xtask = "run --locked --package xtask --"
+
+# A warning that survives to the end of a build is a failure, whoever emitted it.
+#
+# This is not a second statement of the lint wall. The wall in `Cargo.toml`
+# decides WHICH lints warn and is inherited by each member that asks; this
+# decides that a surviving warning is fatal whether or not the unit that emitted
+# it asked for anything. That matters because the check proving inheritance
+# matches manifest text rather than manifest structure, so a member could carry
+# the right bytes in a comment and still build outside the wall. This closes the
+# consequence of that weakness without pretending to fix the check.
+#
+# MEASURED on cargo 1.97.1, in a scratch workspace built for the purpose:
+#   - it denies rustc warnings under `cargo build` and `cargo test`;
+#   - it denies clippy warnings under `cargo clippy`;
+#   - it denies rustdoc warnings under `cargo doc`;
+#   - it denies them in a member that inherits NO `[lints]` table at all, which
+#     is the case the lint-wall check exists to catch and the one this covers
+#     independently;
+#   - it denies them in a path dependency that is not a workspace member.
+#
+# MEASURED not to cover, and each of these is a real ceiling rather than a
+# quibble:
+#   - Cargo's OWN warnings. An unused manifest key prints `warning: … unused
+#     manifest key` and the build still exits 0. A misspelled manifest key is
+#     therefore still silent, which is exactly the failure mode that dependency
+#     inheritance introduces.
+#   - Registry dependencies, which cargo builds with `--cap-lints allow` and
+#     which therefore emit nothing to deny. Measured on this tree: of the three
+#     rustc invocations that build the services, the two that compile a registry
+#     crate carry that flag and the one that compiles a workspace crate does
+#     not. This is why installing a tool from the registry cannot be broken by
+#     this setting.
+#   - A stale `clippy.toml` entry. Clippy's complaint that a configured path no
+#     longer resolves is counted in the tally line and does NOT fail the build:
+#     measured alone, with this setting on, the run exits 0.
+#
+# And one difference in KIND, not coverage: `-D warnings` makes a warning a
+# compile error, so rustc produces no artifact. This counts warnings and fails
+# afterwards, so the artifact exists and dependent units may already have been
+# built against it. It is a gate, not a compiler setting.
+#
+# WHY THE DOCUMENTATION STAGE STILL SETS `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, and why removing it is
+# not a repair. The claim that `[lints]` now reaches rustdoc, so the stage's
+# explicit `RUSTDOCFLAGS = "-D warnings"` could go and close an
+# environment-dependence violation, was tested and is backwards. `[lints]` does
+# reach rustdoc — measured: with the wall inherited and no `RUSTDOCFLAGS` set, a
+# broken intra-doc link fails `cargo doc` with rustdoc printing `-D
+# rustdoc::broken-intra-doc-links` implied by `-D warnings`, and with the wall
+# removed the same source only warns and exits 0. But an AMBIENT `RUSTDOCFLAGS`
+# defeats the wall entirely: measured, `--cap-lints allow` and `-A warnings`
+# each turn that same failing build into an exit 0. Setting the variable for the
+# child is what makes the stage immune to whatever the host has exported; it is
+# a shield, not a dependence, and deleting it would introduce the very
+# environment-dependence it was said to remove.
+[build]
+warnings = "deny"

+#
+# This is NOT the entry bar. `cargo xtask qualify` is the entry bar and the only
+# spelling of it, and every stage of it compiles, tests, or reads this tree with
+# the pinned toolchain and nothing else. cargo-deny is a separately installed
+# binary, so folding it into qualify would make the bar depend on what a machine
+# happens to have installed. It runs here instead, beside the bar, on a host
+# nobody configured.

+# Two jobs, and the split is the point. The graph job reads THIS tree and
+# nothing else, so its result is about the tree alone — the same property qualify
+# states about itself — and it belongs on every pull request, and on every direct
+# push to the trunk for as long as a direct push to the trunk is possible at all.
+# It runs cargo-deny twice: once against `deny.toml`, which must pass, and once
+# against `deny-reversal.toml`, which must REFUSE. A gate that has only ever been
+# seen to pass is a gate whose refusal nobody has watched, so the second run is
+# the one that makes the first one mean something. The advisory job reads a
+# database that moves without this repository changing, so it would turn red on a
+# morning when nothing here changed and green again the same way. That is a
+# useful alarm and a broken gate, so it runs on its own schedule, where red means
+# "go look" rather than "this change is bad".

+
+on:
+  pull_request:
+  # And direct pushes to the trunk: the same trigger that

+  # same opening condition — which is written out once, there, rather than twice

+  # required to pass before a merge exactly as `qualify` is, but only one of the
+  # two carried the bootstrap cover, and nothing anywhere stated a reason for the
+  # difference. A gate that a direct push walks past is not a gate, whatever it
+  # reports on the pull requests it does see. The two triggers were added for one
+  # unexecuted refusal and they retire together.

+    branches: [main]
+  # Weekly, and on demand. The advisory job needs a trigger that is not a change,
+  # because the thing it watches is not in this repository.
+  schedule:
+    - cron: "0 6 * * 1"
+  workflow_dispatch:
+
+# One live run per ref, EXCEPT on the trunk. Cancelling a superseded pull-request
+# run costs nothing, because a newer commit on the same branch is the thing to
+# judge. Cancelling the trunk's own run destroys the record of whether a merged
+# commit held, and that record is the only one nobody can reconstruct later.

+

+          rustup toolchain install

+

+      # `advisories` is deliberately absent from this list — see the schedule
+      # job below, and the note in `deny.toml`.

+
+      # THE PLANTED REVERSAL. The step above establishes that the graph is
+      # lawful today; it cannot establish that the rules still bite, because a
+      # rule that quietly stopped matching prints the same `ok` as a rule that
+      # checked everything. `deny-reversal.toml` is a deliberately wrong
+      # configuration, and this step fails the job when cargo-deny SUCCEEDS
+      # against it.
+      #
+      # BOTH the exit code and the diagnostic are required, because neither is
+      # enough on its own. MEASURED: a usage error — a flag in the wrong
+      # position, a subcommand cargo-deny stopped accepting — also exits 2, so
+      # the code alone would accept a run that never read the configuration at

+      # means the rule refused for the reason that was planted.
+      #
+      # WHAT THIS COVERS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT is written in
+      # `deny-reversal.toml`, beside the defect: it covers `[[bans.features]]`

+      #

+          echo "the planted reversal refused: exit 2, exact-features-mismatch"

+    # Only on the schedule and by hand. This job is an alarm, not a gate: its

+    #
+    # Named by what it RUNS ON rather than by what it skips, and that is the

+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

+      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

+          persist-credentials: false
+

+      # why it is not on a pull request: its answer depends on when it ran.

+# Reporting a security issue
+
+**Report privately, through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting**, on this
+repository's Security tab. That road is private by construction, so a report and
+its repair can be written in the same place without the issue being public
+first. If it is unavailable to you, open an ordinary issue that says only that
+you have something to report and asks for a private channel — no detail, no
+reproduction.
+
+Expect an acknowledgement. There is no service commitment behind that sentence
+and there will not be one until this repository has a release to stand behind:
+this is a small project, and a response time nobody can hold to is worse than no
+number at all.
+
+## What is supported
+
+Nothing yet. Every package here is version `0.0.0`, no version has been
+published, and the repository is in architecture closure — the machine's homes
+carry their specifications and the tooling that checks them, and product runtime
+behaviour is deliberately absent. There is no supported release, so there is no
+supported-versions table; the only thing that can be reported against is the
+trunk as it stands.
+
+This section becomes a table the day a version is published, and not before. A
+table listing supported versions of software nobody can install would be a claim
+about a promise that does not exist.
+
+## What is in scope
+
+The repository as it stands, which today means its tooling and its hosted
+qualification road rather than a running machine:
+
+- the qualification road and the repository laws — a check that can be made to
+  report PASS about a tree it did not read is a defect of exactly the kind this
+  file is for, and so is one that can be made to write into the tree it is
+  judging;
+- the dependency posture — what `deny.toml` allows, what the manifests pin, and
+  any road by which the resolved graph can come to differ from what the
+  repository declares;
+- the hosted workflows — anything that lets a change execute code the
+  repository did not commit, or lets a run reach a credential;
+- the metaprogramming services and the expansion shell — an expansion is
+  supposed to be a function of its declared input alone, and a way to make one
+  read the network, the filesystem, the environment, a clock, or entropy is a
+  report;
+- resource exhaustion driven by an attacker-controlled declaration — an input
+  this repository accepts that can be made to exhaust CPU, memory, stack, or
+  I/O in practice. It is a report whether or not a bound has already been
+  declared for the road it takes. Bounds are being established home by home, so
+  the likeliest place for a finding to land is a road nobody has bounded yet —
+  and a gap in our own coverage is the reason to tell us, never a reason to
+  turn the report away. What a declared bound decides is triage and repair: a
+  crossed bound is a refusal that failed to hold, an absent one is a refusal
+  nobody wrote yet, and the two want different fixes. Neither decides whether
+  the finding belongs here.
+
+## What is not in scope, and why
+
+- **Anything requiring `unsafe`.** The lint wall forbids it outright, so a
+  report that begins by adding it is a report about a different repository.
+- **Findings from a scanner, unaccompanied.** A rule identifier and a file path
+  are not a report. What is needed is the road: what an attacker controls, what
+  they reach, and what they get.
+- **Anything about a host.** Hosts live in other repositories and pin an exact
+  revision of this one. A defect in how a host uses this machine is a report to
+  that host.
+
+## What helps
+
+The exact commit, the exact toolchain, the exact command, and the smallest
+input that shows the behaviour. If the finding is a refusal that should have
+happened and did not, say which refusal — this repository is built out of
+refusals with names, and naming the one that stayed quiet is most of the work.
+Where no refusal covers the road you found, say that instead: a road with no
+refusal on it is a report we want, and finding the name it should have had is
+our job rather than yours.

+#
+# `deny.toml` settles what the resolved graph is allowed to be, and the hosted

+#
+# So this file runs beside the lawful one, and the workflow fails the job when
+# cargo-deny SUCCEEDS here. What it changes is one thing: `syn`'s exact
+# allow-list names a feature the graph does not hold, and omits every feature
+# the graph does hold. That is the mismatch in both directions at once — a list
+# reaching past the graph, and a graph reaching past the list — which is the
+# entire content of `exact = true`. cargo-deny reports it as
+# `exact-features-mismatch` and exits 2, and the workflow requires both.

+# WHY THIS RULE AND NOT ANOTHER. The exact-feature rule is the one that refused
+# the first time it ran against this workspace, against prose here that had
+# claimed a feature cut the graph did not hold. It is the only rule in
+# `deny.toml` with a record of catching a false claim in our own manifests, so
+# it is the one whose continued biting is worth a committed reversal.

+#
+#     licences            the `[licenses] allow` list
+#     sources             `unknown-registry`, `unknown-git`, `allow-registry`
+#     multiple versions   `[bans] multiple-versions`
+#     wildcards           `[bans] wildcards`

+# What the resolved dependency graph is allowed to be.
+#
+# The manifests declare what this workspace ASKS FOR. This file settles what the
+# graph actually IS, and the two are different questions: Cargo unifies features
+# across a build, so a crate nobody here named can switch a feature on in a crate
+# everybody here uses, and every manifest still reads exactly as it did. Three
+# paragraphs in this repository claimed a feature cut that only a manifest can
+# request and only a graph can hold; this file is where that claim is settled
+# against the graph, and it settled it by refusing the first time it ran.
+#
+# THE CEILING ON EVERY FEATURE CLAIM BELOW. Three facts collapse into one
+# sentence the moment nobody keeps them apart, and only the middle one is settled
+# here:
+#
+#     manifest request            what a member's dependency entry asks for
+#     resolved graph union        what the resolver enables for a package across
+#                                 the whole build — what this file settles
+#     compiled-unit feature set   what one rustc invocation is actually handed
+#
+# A `[[bans.features]]` rule reads the resolved graph. It therefore proves the
+# second and does NOT prove the third: a graph holding a feature does not say
+# which compiled unit carries it, and nothing in this repository executes a check
+# that reads the unit graph. The distinction collapses in exactly one case — an
+# EMPTY exact set — because a unit's features are a subset of what the graph
+# resolved, and a subset of nothing is nothing. That is why the `blake3` rule
+# below is stronger in KIND than the `syn` rule and not merely stricter, and why
+# no prose in this tree may read the `syn` rule as a statement about the unit any
+# particular reader links.
+#
+# Adopting this costs a tool the qualification road does not carry. `cargo deny`
+# is not a stage of `cargo xtask qualify`, because qualify's stages compile,
+# test, and read THIS tree with the pinned toolchain and nothing else, and a
+# check that needs a separately installed binary would make the entry bar depend
+# on what a working machine happens to have. It runs beside the bar in the hosted
+# workflow instead, where the host is one nobody configured.
+#
+# A run of this file reports `ok`, and an `ok` is not evidence that anything here
+# still refuses. `deny-reversal.toml` sits beside this file carrying one
+# deliberately wrong rule; the same hosted workflow runs cargo-deny against it
+# and fails the job if cargo-deny succeeds. That reversal covers the `syn`
+# exact-feature rule below and NOTHING else in this file — which rules are left
+# standing on a positive run alone is stated in the reversal itself, where a
+# reader deciding whether to trust a green log will be looking.
+
+[graph]
+# Dependencies a test brings in are dependencies. cargo-deny leaves them out by
+# default, and what its default drops here is the subtree under the
+# compile-refusal harness. A licence rule that cannot see that part of the graph
+# is a licence rule about the part it likes.
+#
+# HOW MUCH of the graph that is, is deliberately not written down. A crate total
+# is a fact about a resolved graph, so it moves with every dependency edit, and
+# a total recorded in a comment goes stale while cargo-deny stays exactly as
+# correct as it was. Anyone who needs the number obtains it: `cargo deny
+# --workspace list` under this line and again with `exclude-dev = true` prints
+# both sets, and `cargo metadata` prints the resolution Cargo itself performs.
+exclude-dev = false
+
+[licenses]
+# The workspace publishes under `MIT OR Apache-2.0`, so a dependency whose terms
+# cannot travel under both cannot travel here. The list is exhaustive by
+# construction: cargo-deny refuses any licence not on it, so a GPL or AGPL
+# arrival anywhere in the graph — including one that appears three levels down
+# in a transitive edge nobody chose — fails rather than warns. Every entry below
+# was MEASURED in the current graph with `cargo deny --workspace list`; nothing
+# is listed in anticipation.
+allow = [
+    "Apache-2.0",
+    "Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception",
+    "BSD-2-Clause",
+    "CC0-1.0",
+    "MIT",
+    "MIT-0",
+    "Unicode-3.0",
+]
+
+[bans]
+# Two copies of one crate at two versions is two decoders, two hash
+# implementations, or two definitions of one type, and the build says nothing
+# about it. The graph carries none today.
+multiple-versions = "deny"
+# A `*` requirement is a decision deferred to whoever resolves next.
+wildcards = "deny"
+# A path dependency carries no version requirement, and inside one checkout that
+# is exactly right: the path IS the resolution. It stops being right the moment
+# the package is published, because a registry resolves nothing by path — which
+# is why this allowance does not extend to publishable crates, and why the two
+# publishable manifests here now carry a version requirement beside their path.
+allow-wildcard-paths = true
+
+# The decoder both readers read Rust through.
+#
+# MEASURED, and it is the whole reason this file exists: the graph holds
+# features the manifests never asked for. `clone-impls`, `derive`,
+# `printing` and `proc-macro` arrive through `serde_derive`, which the
+# compile-refusal harness pulls in as a development dependency. `cargo tree`
+# shows those four resolving on the proc-macro side of the graph, away from the
+# entry the repository's own readers inherit — but that is an OBSERVATION made by
+# hand at one moment, which no gate re-runs and which this file does not carry.
+# The list below answers the question this file is for and stops there: what the
+# graph holds. `exact = true` means any movement at all fails, in either
+# direction, from any source — a reader that stopped needing `full`, and a new
+# dependency that switched on `fold`, `visit`, or `extra-traits`, are the same
+# refusal.
+[[bans.features]]
+crate = "syn"
+allow = ["clone-impls", "derive", "full", "parsing", "printing", "proc-macro"]
+exact = true
+

+#
+# The empty set is the claim: no default features, and nothing any other crate
+# in the graph turned on. `std` would buy an `io::Write` adapter and the
+# error-trait impls; `rayon` would stand a thread pool up inside `rustc`;
+# `serde`, `zeroize`, `mmap` and the digest-trait previews buy surfaces neither
+# crate has a seat for. An empty exact set is the strongest form this mechanism
+# has, because every one of those is a refusal rather than an absence nobody
+# checked. It is also the one rule in this file that reaches past the graph to
+# the compiled unit, for the subset reason stated at the top: no unit can be
+# handed a feature the graph never resolved.
+[[bans.features]]
+crate = "blake3"
+allow = []
+exact = true
+
+[sources]
+# A crate arriving from anywhere but the one registry named below, or from any
+# git remote at all, is a supply chain this repository never decided on.
+unknown-registry = "deny"
+unknown-git = "deny"
+allow-registry = ["https://github.com/rust-lang/crates.io-index"]
+allow-git = []
+
+[advisories]
+# Deliberately no `ignore` entries and no configuration beyond this note.
+#
+# The advisory check is NOT part of the required gate, and the reason is a
+# property the qualification road states about itself: a result is about the
+# tree alone. The advisory database moves on its own schedule, so a required
+# check that reads it turns red on a morning when nothing in the repository
+# changed, and green again on a morning when nothing changed either. That is a
+# useful alarm and a broken gate, so it runs on a schedule of its own, where
+# turning red means "go look" rather than "this change is bad".

+//! until this law was registered they stood outside every denominator the
+//! repository publishes: the red ledgers in `crate::checks::obligations` count
+//! testpak's tests and its compile-fail fixtures, and a configuration beside a
+//! hosted workflow is neither. Deleting the reversal moved no number and failed
+//! no check, so qualification kept reading whole after the checker had
+//! disappeared.
+//!
+//! That gap was already WRITTEN DOWN, in the reversal's own prose, and writing
+//! a gap down does not close it. Prose keeps reading as true after the thing it
+//! describes is gone — which is the single failure the whole obligations join
+//! was built to refuse, arriving one file to the side of the join.
+//!
+//! # What is claimed here, and the name that came down to claim it
+//!
+//! Four facts about FILES: the workflow file is committed, the rule set is
+//! committed, the reversal is committed, and the reversal states something that
+//! is not byte-for-byte the rule set. The gate's artifacts are PRESENT and
+//! VISIBLY DISTINCT. That is the whole claim, and the roster entry now says so
+//! in those words.

+//! control that CAN be widened to cover its name is widened, and the name
+//! stands. This one cannot be: establishing that a workflow still invokes the
+//! reversal means reading the workflow, that means a YAML reader this repository
+//! has not admitted, and the alternative — matching text in a workflow file — is
+//! the class of reader `crate::checks::obligations` has now replaced four
+//! separate times, each replacement made because a semantic category recognized
+//! by a convenient spelling is a category the next spelling walks past. So the
+//! claim came down to the body rather than the body being sent up to the claim,
+//! and what this law is called is now what this law establishes.
+//!
+//! # Where the gate is counted, and why here
+//!
+//! In the roster `main.rs` holds, which that file states is the only statement
+//! of how many repository laws there are. The gate occupies one line of it:
+//! present, the run prints one more PASS than it did; deleted along with this
+//! law, the roster is one shorter and the deletion is a line of a diff nobody
+//! can miss; deleted on its own, this law FAILS and takes stage four of

+//! one seat shorter or longer only when a law arrives or goes, and a claim
+//! narrowed to its evidence is neither.

+//! The reversal LEDGER was the other seat considered, and it lost on what it
+//! would have cost. Admitting a committed artifact that is not a testpak test
+//! into the red population means loosening the resolver that ledger's exactness

+//! the loosening would apply to every `red:` row in every home, not to the one
+//! row that wanted it. It would also have to be written in a tooling ledger

+//! seated in a home that does not own it is the duplicate authority this
+//! repository is eliminating, bought at the price of a weaker join over a
+//! published number.

+//! # What this law reads, and it is not a parse

+//! Three files are present, the reversal states something, and the reversal is
+//! not byte-for-byte the rule set it stands against. That is the whole reading:
+//! four facts about files, no grammar entered, no line matched, no structure

+    /// invokes nothing at all still passes this law.
+    ///
+    /// It proves nothing about the gate, and it is not a positive control. What
+    /// it holds in place is the NAME. The fixture workflow here carries no job
+    /// and no step, exactly as a workflow somebody edited the reversal step out
+    /// of carries none, and this law is content with both — which is the fail
+    /// open the module documentation states. A later reader who widens this law
+    /// to read what a hosted run executed has to delete this test to do it, and
+    /// that deletion is the line of the diff where the claim is allowed to grow
+    /// back.
+    #[test]
+    fn a_workflow_that_invokes_nothing_still_passes() {
+        let scratch = planted("gate-workflow-invokes-nothing");
+        scratch.write(
+            &GATE_WORKFLOW.join("/"),
+            "name: dependencies\non:\n  pull_request:\njobs: {}\n",
+        );
+        let found = check_dependency_gate_artifacts(scratch.root());
+        assert!(
+            found.is_ok(),
+            "this law reads files and not steps; a verdict here would mean it had started reading \
+             steps without its name saying so: {found:?}"
+        );
+    }
+
+    /// The real repository holds: the gate's three artifacts are committed, and
+    /// the reversal states something that is not the rule set.
+    #[test]
+    fn the_real_gate_artifacts_are_present_and_distinct() {
+        let root = repo_root().unwrap_or_else(|_| PathBuf::from("."));
+        let found = check_dependency_gate_artifacts(&root);
+        assert!(found.is_ok(), "{found:?}");
+    }
+}

Foundation Closure B5 — toolchain and CI governance. Draft: nothing here has been run on a hosted host yet, and one of the six commits changes what a hosted run attempts. ## Lead with what is unproven - **No hosted run exists for any of this.** The Windows leg is added but has never executed on a runner. `cargo xtask qualify` is green on a Windows working machine, which is a different host and a weaker claim. - **cargo-deny is not a stage of the entry bar.** It runs beside it, so a working machine that never installs it never learns any of what it enforces. Until branch protection requires the new workflow, its refusals stand beside a merge button rather than in front of it. - **`build.warnings = "deny"` fires on nothing in this tree today.** Every member inherits the wall already. Pure addition; the cost is paid for a case that does not currently exist. - **`disallowed-methods` is NOT adopted.** The measured population is 40 sites, 37 of them the silent-skip class across three crates. Recorded as a refusal with its numbers and its opening condition. - **`push: [main]` stays.** It is retired by a branch-protection setting that forbids the direct push it exists to catch, never by deleting the line. - **Branch protection needs updating for the matrix.** The required check is no longer `qualify`; it is `qualify (ubuntu-latest)` and `qualify (windows-latest)`. ## The measurement that reversed a planned repair The plan was to delete `RUSTDOCFLAGS = "-D warnings"` from the documentation stage, on the finding that `[lints]` now forwards to rustdoc. The first half is true and was re-measured: with the wall inherited and no `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, a broken intra-doc link fails `cargo doc`; with the wall removed the same source warns and exits 0. **The conclusion is backwards.** An ambient `RUSTDOCFLAGS` defeats the wall outright — `--cap-lints allow` and `-A warnings` each turn that failing build into an exit 0. Setting the variable for the child is a shield against the host, not a dependence on it, and removing it would introduce the environment dependence it was said to close. `RUSTDOCFLAGS` stays, and the measurement is written down beside the warning configuration. ## The measurement that earned cargo-deny Three manifests claimed `syn` runs with `full` and `parsing` and that printing, folding, visiting, derive input, extra traits and the proc-macro bridge are off. Against the resolved graph the enabled set is **six**. The four extra arrive through `serde_derive`, which the compile-refusal harness pulls in; under resolver 3 they land on a separate compiled unit, so the prose was true about what the manifests ASK FOR and false about what the graph HOLDS. Nothing in the repository could tell those apart. `[[bans.features]] exact = true` refused the first time it ran. Two more day-one catches: cargo-deny's default graph is 21 crates against `cargo metadata`'s 44 (the absent 23 are the dev subtree — closed with `exclude-dev = false`), and `wildcards = "deny"` found two publishable crates reaching their dependencies by path alone, which resolves inside a checkout and nowhere else. ## Commits 1. `4c57807` — one `[workspace.dependencies]` table; members inherit; `trybuild` exact-pinned. `Cargo.lock` and every resolved feature set unchanged. 2. `2a75779` — `deny.toml` plus a `dependencies` workflow. Advisories on their own schedule, deliberately not in the required list. 3. `1fda2ef` — the MSRV contradiction closed by deleting a claim: `1.97` becomes `1.97.1` in two files, and `one-toolchain-floor` joins all four statements. 4. `365f91f` — `build.warnings = "deny"`, with its coverage and its ceilings measured; `RUSTDOCFLAGS` kept. 5. `c80a347` — Windows leg, `timeout-minutes`, concurrency fixed so the trunk stops cancelling itself, weekly run with its claim stated, `SECURITY.md`. 6. `c5e0c73` — `disallowed-methods` refused on the record, with counts. ## Executed evidence `cargo xtask qualify` — all 7 stages hold, on a Windows working machine, on the committed tree. `cargo deny --workspace --locked check bans licenses sources` — ok, with five planted reversals each refusing with its own exit code. ## Two lines of xtask changed outside this boundary `xtask/src/checks/toolchain.rs` (the reading) and `xtask/src/main.rs` (the registration string). Named here because another boundary owns that crate. ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Added automated dependency license, source, duplication, and feature-policy checks. - Added scheduled and on-demand security advisory scans. - Added supply-chain validation to qualification checks. - Qualification now runs across Ubuntu and Windows. - **Documentation** - Added security vulnerability reporting guidance. - Clarified dependency, toolchain, qualification, and workflow expectations. - **Bug Fixes** - Improved toolchain consistency checks to detect mismatches across project configuration.

Greptile Summary

This change centralizes Rust workspace policy, adds dependency-graph governance, and expands qualification coverage across Ubuntu and Windows. The dependency policy accepts the current resolved workspace graph, while the deliberately invalid feature configuration is rejected for the intended reason.

Confidence Score: 5/5

No blocking failure remains. No accepted blocking findings remain after exercising the dependency policy’s normal and deliberately invalid configurations.

T-Rex Logs

 **What T-Rex did** - Ran the focused dependency-governance verification script to validate normal and reversal policy checks. - Observed that the normal dependency graph policy check passed, with bans, licenses, and sources OK. - Demonstrated the planted reversal policy was rejected, emitting exact-features-mismatch and exiting with error. - Completed the end-to-end focused dependency-governance run successfully. Ran code and verified through T-Rex
